name: Ben Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ben Novak, 43, and I run a front-end loader at a large mine. I bring broken rock to the feed hopper, stop for blocked lanes, and clean the cab before the next shift. I'm a junior operator and still make slow turns; my lead driver shows me where I waste movement, and my wife cleans offices early in the morning, and we share school runs for our two children. We have a mortgage and less than a month's expenses saved, so my lower mine wage matters every week. I use AI on my phone every day to quiz myself on machine terms, then check the mine manual before touching anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small AI tools are fine for learning the handbook, but the loader still needs hands on controls. I tell new drivers to verify every answer against the mine's own instructions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine is my best local wage, and our savings wouldn't carry a full month without it. Even if the job stays, I need to get better at loading so my lead driver trusts me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a notebook of loading errors and review it with the lead driver each Thursday. I'd use an AI quiz to practice machine terms after shifts, then verify answers in the mine manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested in the tools, but I feel the mortgage waiting behind every experiment. I can risk getting a quiz answer wrong at home, not a bucket movement near another worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of error goes in the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I approached the hopper too wide and held up a truck behind me. I wrote down the turn and asked my lead driver to watch my next pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new AI service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we cannot afford another subscription. The free quiz is enough while we build a little breathing room.

I tell new drivers to **verify every answer** against the mine's own instructions.
think: The mine is my best **local wage**, and our savings wouldn't carry a full month without it.

do: Keep a **notebook of loading errors** and review it with the lead driver each Thursday.
Use an AI quiz to **practice machine terms** after shifts, then verify answers in the mine manual.
feel: **Anxious** about wages and competence, while interested in low-cost learning tools.
S0.quote: I can risk getting a quiz answer wrong at home, not a bucket movement near another worker.
fieldNote: His daily AI use is **bounded by manual checks** and the real danger of loader movements.
He worries about both **junior competence** and less than a month's household reserve despite the mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep a loading-error notebook and review it each Thursday
Practice machine terms with a free AI quiz and verify the manual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew automated planning might clear the queue if drivers can report blocked lanes. I'd ask for trial runs before the mine changes every loader target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster feed schedule could make my slow turns cost the mine money. If junior shifts are cut, my wife's cleaning hours won't cover our house payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my lead driver to time three loading cycles and show me where I can move safely faster. I'd test the mine's queue display during a supervised shift if the trial is approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one makes me eager and nervous at the same time. I like solving a queue problem, but I know a manager can call a shorter roster an efficiency gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a different post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first see whether the loader trial actually needs an operator beside it. If my hours fell, I'd apply for a paid maintenance helper opening, but I wouldn't claim I'm a mechanic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your wife think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would ask whether the new targets pay extra or just make me rush. We have learned that a long shift does not always mean a larger pay packet.

I'd ask for **trial runs** before the mine changes every loader target.

do: Ask my lead driver to **time three loading cycles** and show me where I can move safely faster.
Test the mine's **queue display** during a supervised shift if the trial is approved.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer junior shifts, with energy for supervised trials.
S1.quote: We have learned that a long shift does not always mean a larger pay packet.
fieldNote: He sees **planning software** as a possible queue improvement while recognising a risk to junior hours.
His maintenance interest is **conditional on lost hours** and a paid opening; he does not claim repair skill.

steps.text: Time three loading cycles with the lead driver
Test the queue display during a supervised approved trial
Apply for a paid maintenance helper opening if loader hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 will change the office first; loaders still need operators until robots arrive. I'd ask which robot loaders the mine plans to try around 2031 and who can train on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, I may get three years to turn my curiosity into another paid skill. The mine could automate loaders faster than I can pay down our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training manager about a paid equipment-service course before the end of this year. I'd keep driving the loader in 2029 while applying for a junior service assistant opening if one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would move quickly, because I can see a date on this picture. I'm frightened that the training queue will be longer than the robot delivery schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why equipment service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like finding why a machine loses power, but I only know the operator checks today. A paid course would let me learn from a mechanic instead of pretending an AI answer is a repair license.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the service course is full?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my loader wages and ask my church friend, who repairs farm equipment, if his shop has paid helper work. I wouldn't move the family on the hope of a vacancy.

I'd ask which **robot loaders** the mine plans to try around 2031 and who can train on them.
think: At **45 in 2028**, I may get three years to turn my curiosity into another paid skill.
The mine could automate loaders faster than I can pay down our **mortgage**.
do: Ask the training manager about a **paid equipment-service course** before the end of this year.
Keep driving the **loader in 2029** while applying for a junior service assistant opening if one exists.
feel: **Alarmed** by robot loaders threatening wages before a new trade is secure.
S2.quote: I'm frightened that the training queue will be longer than the robot delivery schedule.
fieldNote: He identifies the **2028 thinking change** separately from the 2031 threat to loader operation.
His course and service move depend on **paid places**; a church contact is only a backup inquiry.

steps.text: Enrol in a paid equipment-service course if the mine offers a place
Keep paid loader shifts during 2029 while applying for service openings
Apply for a junior service assistant opening if one exists
Ask a church friend about paid farm-equipment helper work if training is full

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children the five-year warning means I can learn a trade before robots drive the loaders. I'd ask the mine for paid training dates rather than a promise that jobs will appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 in 2031, and robots could reach my loader around 2034. Five years could build a cushion, but our school and mortgage bills won't pause for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put half of each overtime payment into a separate savings account starting this month. I'd apply for the mine's paid electrical apprentice intake if it opens next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have enough time to make a fair attempt, though not enough to be careless. I would tell my wife about each application before I tell the children we have a new plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would electrical work stay safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know; the robots might do parts of wiring or testing later. I would want the apprenticeship to include real fault finding and safe work around machines, not only button pressing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue paid work in the mine and check whether the apprentice intake actually led to jobs. If it hadn't, I'd ask a local electrical contractor about a paid trainee place before the loaders change.

Apply for the mine's **paid electrical apprentice** intake if it opens next spring.
feel: **Anxious** about training outcomes, but able to build a small reserve over five years.
S3.quote: I would tell my wife about each application before I tell the children we have a new plan.
fieldNote: His five-year plan combines **overtime savings** and a conditional paid apprenticeship.
He resists promising a new future to his **children** until an actual training route leads to wages.

steps.text: Save half of each overtime payment in a separate account
Apply for the paid electrical apprentice intake if it opens
Keep paid mine work during the first year after 2031
Ask a local electrical contractor about paid training if mine placements fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade of warning gives working people time to earn a second skill. I'd support paid apprenticeships that lead to real service jobs when robots enter the mine around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, I may still need many years of income, even if our children are grown. I cannot count on a pension that I have never seen in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the mine's paid controls apprenticeship details this quarter and apply if entry is open. I'd make a small mortgage overpayment each month that my wife and I both work full schedules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade feels like a chance to become useful at more than one machine. I would still keep a hand on the family budget, because a certificate is not the same as a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for in that apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to work beside a technician on sensors and motor controls, with proper safety instruction. My phone can help me study terms, but it cannot sign off a repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep earning in the mine or a service shop while robot loaders spread toward 2039. If controls work also shrank, I'd look for paid repair work outside mining rather than wait for the last loader shift.

say: I'd say a **decade of warning** gives working people time to earn a second skill.
I'd support **paid apprenticeships** that lead to real service jobs when robots enter the mine around 2039.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I may still need many years of income, even if our children are grown.
I cannot count on a **pension** that I have never seen in writing.
do: Request the mine's **paid controls apprenticeship** details this quarter and apply if entry is open.
Make a small **mortgage overpayment** each month that my wife and I both work full schedules.
feel: **Uneasy** about the end point, with time for paid training and gradual debt reduction.
S4.quote: I would still keep a hand on the family budget, because a certificate is not the same as a wage.
fieldNote: He is more willing than a reluctant worker to pursue **controls training**, while checking whether it leads to paid jobs.
His children may be grown by the robot date, yet **mortgage and living costs** persist.

steps.text: Apply for a paid controls apprenticeship if mine entry opens
Make small mortgage overpayments in months with two full schedules
Keep earning in mine or service work after 2036
Look for paid repair work outside mining if controls jobs shrink

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest because a junior loader driver might only have three years before robot machines reach the pit. Paid service training with a published intake date and a real job at the end would help me use those years. My wife and I would also need a way to cover the mortgage during classes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a trainee can fail a course and try again without losing their shift. I study hard, but I'm still learning the loader, one exam should not wipe out my family's income.

headlineQuote: one exam should not wipe out my family's income.
portrait: Ben is a **43-year-old junior** loader operator at a large mine who studies machine terms after shifts.
His wife's office-cleaning hours, two school-age children, a **mortgage**, and scant savings make paid hours essential.
He uses **AI daily** for quizzes but checks the mine manual and asks experienced staff before acting.
He seeks **paid service training** early and watches whether any new certificate leads to lasting wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives him only three years before robot loaders may threaten his junior wage.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid service place**, published intake date, and actual job path would make training possible alongside the mortgage.
